scenes.narration: Nearly every disaster-recovery question on both AWS exams is the same puzzle wearing a different costume. The scenario hands you two numbers: how long the system can stay down, and how much data it can afford to lose. Those are R T O, recovery time objective, and R P O, recovery point objective. This chapter maps to Design Resilient Architectures, twenty six percent of the associate exam, and Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions, twenty five percent of the professional exam. Between the two, disaster recovery is worth close to a quarter of everything you will see on exam day, which is why it earns a full chapter instead of a paragraph inside general resilience.

facts.label: RTO — Recovery Time Objective
facts.value: How long the business can tolerate being down

facts.label: RPO — Recovery Point Objective
facts.value: How much data, measured in time, it can afford to lose

scenes.narration: Ask a room of candidates to design for disaster recovery, and two reflexes show up almost every time, often from the same person in the same breath. The first: 'we already run Multi, A, Z, so we already have disaster recovery' — which feels right because Multi-AZ genuinely does make things more resilient, just not to the failure this term is actually testing. The second: faced with four unfamiliar tiers, defaulting to whichever one sounds the most bulletproof, usually a full multi-region active-active design, on the theory that more resilience can never be the wrong answer. There's a quieter third version of the same mistake: wiring a fast-recovering application tier to a database that only backs up once a night, and calling the whole thing fast, without checking which piece actually sets the real recovery numbers.

props.heading: "We run Multi-AZ, so we're already covered"
bullets: Treating a Multi-AZ database as automatic disaster recovery — it survives one data center failing, not an entire Region.
Defaulting to the fanciest-sounding tier, multi-site active/active, on the theory that more resilience can never be wrong.
Wiring a fast application tier to a database that only backs up nightly, and calling the whole design fast.

scenes.narration: Every disaster-recovery question, at either exam level, is really asking you to solve for two variables. How long can the business tolerate being down, measured from the moment of failure to the moment service is restored — that's your downtime number. And how much data, measured in time, can the business tolerate losing — the gap between the last safely captured copy and the moment things broke. Neither number comes from the architecture; a finance team, a compliance rule, or a customer contract states them, and the architecture's whole job is to satisfy both at the lowest cost that actually works. Underline both before you even glance at the answer options — almost every wrong answer in this domain is wrong for exactly one reason: it quietly blows past one of these two.

props.kicker: THE TWO NUMBERS BEHIND EVERY DR QUESTION

scenes.narration: Multi-AZ replicates synchronously to a standby in a different facility, but that facility still sits inside the very same AWS Region — so it's built to survive one data center going dark, nothing bigger. A scenario asking your system to survive an entire Region disappearing is a completely different failure domain, and no amount of Multi-AZ configuration inside that one Region touches it; that calls for one of the four cross-region tiers coming up next. The trap is that both scenarios can be described using almost identical, comforting language — 'the app must stay available' — so read carefully for whether the failure named is one facility or a whole Region before you even look at the options.

props.heading: Multi-AZ vs. cross-region DR — not the same question

scenes.narration: Here are the four disaster-recovery strategies both exams organize around, ordered from cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest. Underneath all four, there are really just two dials: how much of the data layer stays continuously replicated, and how much of the compute layer stays continuously running. Backup and restore turns both dials to zero — nothing runs until disaster strikes, and recovery stretches from hours toward a full day. Pilot light turns the data dial up but leaves compute at zero, recovering in tens of minutes to a few hours. Warm standby turns both dials up partway, with a small, already-running fleet cutting that down to minutes. And multi-site active-active turns both dials all the way up in both directions, running full duplicate capacity in two or more Regions at once for a near-zero recovery time and near-zero data loss.

rows.label: Pilot Light
cells: Tens of minutes to a few hours

scenes.narration: This is the single most exam-relevant habit in the whole chapter: read a scenario's two numbers, then walk these four tiers starting from the cheapest, and stop at the very first one that clears both bars. If a day of downtime and a day of lost data are both genuinely fine, backup and restore is already the answer — anything pricier is money spent on a requirement nobody stated. If the business can't absorb more than a few minutes down, you're past pilot light and into warm standby. And multi-site active-active only becomes correct once a scenario ties a near-zero requirement to an explicit, budgeted business justification — 'this workload is important' is never, on its own, that justification.

scenes.narration: You won't be asked to write this syntax from memory on either exam, but you should recognize what each piece is for. A script that stands up a cross-region read replica is the data-layer piece pilot light and warm standby both depend on. A separate promote script is the one-way door — run only during a genuine failover, because once a replica is promoted, there's no undoing it without rebuilding replication from scratch. A Route 53 failover record is the routing layer, redirecting traffic once a health check actually detects the primary is down. And a backup plan handles the fourth tier entirely on its own — though it only counts as real cross-region protection once it explicitly copies backups into a second Region; a retention setting alone doesn't get you there.

props.kicker: THE FILES BEHIND A REAL FAILOVER
props.heading: disaster-recovery/

scenes.narration: Here's the operational sequence a team actually runs during a real regional failover. First, promote the DR-region read replica — a permanent, one-way action that turns it into a standalone, writable primary; there's no walking this back. Next, update the Route 53 record so DNS starts answering with the DR region's load balancer instead of the dead primary — but the real recovery time from this step is bounded by the health check's detection interval plus however long client-side DNS caches take to expire, not the instant the command returns. Finally, scale the DR region's Auto Scaling group up from its minimal, always-on size to full production capacity. In warm standby that's a fast scale-out of a fleet that was already running; in pilot light, this same step also has to boot instances from a cold start, which is exactly why pilot light's recovery time runs longer.

orders-db-dr-replica is now a standalone, writable instance
Failover record applied — DNS now answers with the DR region's load balancer
Real propagation time = health-check interval + client DNS cache TTL

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. Northgate Payments runs card-settlement processing under a contract that requires resuming operations within thirty minutes of a regional disaster, and losing no more than five minutes of transaction data. Pilot light looks tempting because it's cheaper, but its typical recovery time — tens of minutes to a few hours, depending on how long compute takes to boot from cold — risks blowing straight through that thirty-minute bound. Warm standby's already-running, scaled-down fleet is the cheapest tier that reliably clears both numbers. A multi-site active-active design would also technically work here, but nothing in the contract ties a near-zero requirement to a stated budget for running full duplicate capacity, so reaching for it anyway would be solving a problem nobody's paying to solve.

props.heading: A payments contract with a hard thirty-minute clock

scenes.narration: Try these yourself before the answers. First: a scenario says a workload has to keep running if a single Availability Zone fails, with no mention of anything region-wide — what's the minimum design that actually satisfies that? Second, and this one catches even people who got the first one right: a team fails over its database in five minutes during a real regional outage, but customers report the outage lasting far longer, because the primary DNS record carries a twenty-four-hour time-to-live. What's actually driving that gap between the infrastructure recovering and customers still seeing an outage?

questions.prompt: A scenario requires a workload to keep running if a single Availability Zone fails, with no mention of a Region-wide event. What's the minimum design that satisfies this?
options: A Multi-AZ deployment within one Region
Backup and restore into a second Region
Pilot light in a second Region

questions.prompt: A team promotes its DR-region database and updates DNS within five minutes during a real regional outage, but customers report the outage lasting far longer — the primary record carries a twenty-four-hour TTL. What's actually causing the gap?
options: Many client DNS resolvers keep answering with the cached record until it expires, so they keep hitting the dead endpoint
The promoted database is corrupted and rejecting new connections
Route 53 health checks take twenty-four hours to detect any failure
TTL only affects write traffic, never read traffic

scenes.narration: Here's why. The Availability Zone question wants a Multi-AZ deployment inside one Region and nothing more — reaching across Regions for an outage that never crosses a Region boundary just spends money against a bar that was already cleared. And the DNS case is the sneakier one: the infrastructure genuinely failed over in minutes, but a long cache lifetime means plenty of client resolvers keep answering with the old, dead address until their own cached copy finally expires — sometimes the better part of a day later. The fix is lowering that time-to-live on any record that participates in failover, well before an incident ever happens, trading a little extra steady-state DNS traffic for a real cut in how long customers actually feel the outage.

answers.prompt: Minimum design for surviving a single AZ failure, with nothing region-wide stated.
answers.correct: A Multi-AZ deployment within one Region.
answers.rationale: The stated failure domain never crosses a Region boundary, so Multi-AZ is already sufficient — every cross-region option spends money solving a problem the scenario never described.

answers.prompt: Why the outage outlasted a five-minute technical failover.
answers.correct: Cached DNS answers kept a chunk of clients pointed at the dead primary until their TTL expired.
answers.rationale: The infrastructure recovered in minutes, but a twenty-four-hour TTL meant plenty of resolvers wouldn't re-query DNS for up to a day. Lowering the TTL on any record that participates in failover, ahead of time, is what actually closes this gap.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. Pull the two numbers straight out of scenario text before you look at the options — nearly every wrong answer breaks one of them quietly. Multi-AZ and cross-region disaster recovery answer two different questions; one survives losing a facility, the other survives losing an entire Region, and neither substitutes for the other. Walk the four tiers cheapest to priciest and stop at the first one that clears both bars — the exam rewards the cheapest sufficient design, never the most resilient one technically possible. Treat any promise of a flatly zero recovery-point number across Regions as a trap unless it's carefully qualified, since real replication always carries some lag. And remember an architecture is only ever as resilient as its slowest-recovering piece — find that piece before trusting the label on everything around it. Next up, chapter fourteen turns this exact same discipline toward a completely different question: how AWS actually prices On-Demand against Reserved Instances and Spot, and why right-sizing comes before any of that.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Pull RTO and RPO straight out of scenario text before reading the options — almost every wrong answer quietly breaks one of them.
Multi-AZ survives an Availability Zone failing; only a cross-region DR tier survives a Region failing — they answer different questions and don't substitute for each other.
Walk the four DR tiers cheapest to priciest and stop at the first one that clears both numbers — the exam rewards the cheapest sufficient answer, never the most resilient one possible.
Cross-region replication is asynchronous almost everywhere — a promised zero RPO across Regions with no qualification is a trap, not a feature.
An architecture is only as resilient as its slowest-recovering component, and the AZ and Region failure domains stack rather than substitute.

scenes.narration: One more to work through yourself. A scenario describes an application tier running multi-site active-active across two Regions, serving live traffic in both at once — but its database only replicates through a nightly backup job. Using this chapter's framework, is it fair to call the whole system multi-site active-active? And what actually determines this system's real recovery time and real recovery point, no matter how fast the front end looks?

props.prompt: An application tier runs multi-site active-active across two Regions, but its database only replicates via a nightly backup job. Is it fair to call the whole system multi-site active-active — and what actually sets its real RTO and RPO?
